title: The Black Umbrella Next Door

beats.t: Three clear days in a row. A high sky, and sun icons across the whole week's forecast.
Yet the woman next door came out with her black umbrella again.
(Umbrella again. Zero percent chance of rain today.)
They stood by the elevator. The woman held the folded umbrella's handle. Her tightly clenched hand was white.
Hello. You brought your umbrella again. I wondered if I'd read the forecast wrong.
It won't rain. I just carry it.
Oh, so like a parasol? To shade you from the sun.
Something like that. The sun stings a little.
The conversation ended there. The elevator numbers descended slowly. Silence grew heavier one floor at a time.
I'm Yeoni. Next door. May I ask your name?
My name... I'll tell you later.
Why? Is it a secret?
Giving someone my name feels like owing them. Giving something when there's nothing to receive is a little...
Behind Yeoni's ear, something tingled. It sounded like something heard before. But where would not come to mind.
(A name as a debt. Who says that? ...And why does it feel familiar?)
The elevator arrived. They entered side by side. Two figures reflected in its mirror. The woman did not look.
You've been here a few days, but I haven't heard a sound. Haven't you unpacked yet?
Not much to unpack. I won't be staying long.
Oh, just a short stay? A business trip or something?
Something like that. I'll leave when the job's finished. I don't know when that will be.
For the first time, the woman looked at Yeoni. Very briefly, as if checking something. Then back to the floor display.
(Why did she look at me like that? Like she was checking whether something had happened to me.)
When the doors opened on the first floor, the woman stepped out first, walking quickly. The black umbrella's tip tapped the floor.
In the playground before the building, a child fell and scraped a knee. The child bit their lip, trying not to cry.
Before Yeoni could run over, the woman stopped. Midstride. Abruptly.
She set down the umbrella and knelt. A bandage came from her coat pocket, as though prepared in advance.
If it hurts a lot, you can cry. Holding it in doesn't make it hurt less.
The child finally cried. The woman did not soothe them. She simply applied the bandage carefully and waited until the crying was done.
(Her voice is cold, but her hands are so careful.)
Her sleeve rode up as she placed the bandage. Something like a thin golden cord flashed at her right wrist. A bracelet, perhaps, but it seemed embedded in the skin.
Perhaps sensing Yeoni's gaze, she pulled down her sleeve. Then picked up her umbrella without a word.
The child must have been really frightened. I'm glad you helped.
Nothing to thank me for. I was just passing.
For someone just passing, she had stopped a long time. Yeoni watched her walk away.
The child's mother ran up and bowed. The woman was already too far away to accept it. As though gratitude were a heavy burden.
(She avoids being thanked. Like hearing thank you would bring disaster.)
The child tugged Yeoni's sleeve and asked the woman's name. Yeoni didn't know, either.
I don't know. I'll be sure to ask next time. Maybe she'll answer then.
At home, Neo waited in the entryway. When Yeoni rolled up a dry sleeve, he tilted his head briefly.
“You met that woman again? You smell of rain.”
It was clear today, dear customer. No possible smell of rain.
“That's what's strange. Someone who smells of rain on a clear day.”
(Right. It is strange. An umbrella in clear weather. Rain scent in clear weather.)
Yeoni sat on the sofa and opened their notes. The list from three days ago. Bread. Luna. Moka. Yundal. Black tiger.
But reading it did not clearly bring back their faces. What color was Moka's tail? Which hand wore Yundal's glove?
Neo. It's already blurring. I can't remember Moka's voice.
“Mine, too, little by little. The longer we're here, the farther away things over there seem.”
Then I'll write more. Faster than it disappears.
Yeoni added lines beneath the list. Moka, otter, bad at rap. Yundal, right-hand glove, compatibility scams. Black tiger, red eyes, a name is a debt.
At the last line, their fingers stopped. A name is a debt. The same shape as the words by the elevator today.
(Could it be? No. That tiger is over there. This is reality.)
“What are you thinking? You look serious.”
Nothing. Just that lots of people in the world have similar ways of speaking.
Yeoni underlined the last word. The phone beside them gave a brief chime. Over a captured image of the notes, a tiny umbrella icon blinked. An unfamiliar symbol.
Late that night, Yeoni went into the corridor with the recycling. The fluorescent light flickered again.
At the window at the corridor's end stood the woman next door. Beneath her open black umbrella. Indoors, on a night without rain.
...Not sleeping? What are you doing there?
The woman slowly turned. Her eyes were dark beneath the umbrella's shadow. But when the light flickered, red flashed in them.
(Red... no. The fluorescent light.)
Go inside. You'll catch a cold.
A cold? It isn't even raining.
You're right. It isn't.
(She's telling me not to get rained on. Even though there's no rain.)
You should go inside, too. The corridor's cold. Standing under an umbrella makes you look even colder.
I'm fine. I need to stand here before I can sleep.
A strange answer. But Yeoni asked no more. It felt as though another question might break her.
Yeoni took the saved half-roll from the bag they carried and quietly placed it on the windowsill.
A midnight snack. Leftover, so it's free. You don't have to eat it.
The woman did not fold her umbrella. Until Yeoni closed the door, she only looked outside. She did not touch the bread.
Only after closing the door did Yeoni realize. Water marks ran along the corridor floor, from the window to the neighbor's door. On a night without one drop of rain.
The next morning, the windowsill was empty. The bread bag hung neatly folded from Yeoni's door handle. No note inside.
